name: Cho gio (cạo gió)

lead: Cạo gió ("scraping wind") is the Vietnamese term for gua sha, a traditional East and Southeast Asian practice of scraping oiled skin with a smooth tool such as a coin or spoon until reddish marks appear.
Traditionally it is a home remedy; its appearance link comes from the facial gua sha trend, where lighter strokes are used for skin refresh and facial contouring.

paras: Traditional cạo gió uses firm, one-direction strokes with a blunt tool over oiled skin until marks appear. Facial gua sha uses lighter pressure with a stone tool.

Treatment nearly always causes some skin trauma such as redness and bruising; burns, infection with unsterilised tools and rare serious injury are reported. The marks have been misread as signs of abuse.

chain: Claimed refreshed, more defined face (facial version)
angle.text: Facial gua sha is used for a refreshed, contoured look; benefits are claimed by practitioners and beauty influencers.

lead: Cạo gió ('scraping wind') is the Vietnamese name for gua sha, a practice in which a blunt, smooth object such as a coin, ceramic spoon, jade stone or buffalo horn is drawn firmly over lubricated skin until red or purple petechiae, called sha, appear. [1] It remains a home remedy in Vietnamese, Cambodian and Indonesian diaspora communities. [1]

The appearance connection is the facial version of gua sha. Practitioners use lighter pressure on the face, and in 2021 and 2022 beauty influencers on TikTok promoted it for lymphatic drainage, a refreshed look and skin rejuvenation, with stone tools sold as skincare accessories. [1] Users of that trend describe a temporarily de-puffed, more sculpted-looking face; the traditional cạo gió is a body treatment for illness and fatigue rather than a cosmetic one. [1]

Research is limited to a 2007 pilot study of microcirculation in healthy subjects, and Wikipedia's article states that gua sha lacks high-quality evidence of clinical benefit. [1][2] The marks it leaves have been mistaken for signs of abuse, which is the most-documented controversy around cạo gió. [1]

paras: Gua means to scrape and sha refers to the marks left behind; in traditional Chinese medicine practitioners link the marks with qi and blood stagnation, and early texts attribute 'sha' syndromes to wind or cold stagnating in the body. [1] The Vietnamese term cạo gió reflects that idea of scraping out 'wind'. [1]

The practice is also known in English as spooning or coining, after the tools used. [1][2] Wikipedia traces it to ancient China and links it with the Shanghan Lun (about 220 CE), with formal use in TCM placed in the Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644). [1]

In general terms, the practitioner applies oil or another lubricant and strokes the skin firmly in one direction with the tool, following muscles or meridians, until petechiae appear. Gua sha is often combined with fire cupping. [1] Pressure is lighter for facial use and firmer for musculoskeletal complaints. [1]

Proponents use it for pain relief, relaxation, colds and fatigue. [1] In Vietnamese households it is commonly done by a family member when someone feels unwell, and the marks are taken to show that the 'wind' has come out. [1]

Facial gua sha uses a flat stone, often jade or rose quartz, with gentle gliding strokes and no intention of raising marks. According to Wikipedia, this version surged on TikTok in 2021 and 2022, when beauty influencers described it as supporting lymphatic drainage and rejuvenating skin, and the trend was covered in a 2022 New York Times article. [1]

Facial gua sha is used for a refreshed, contoured look, and the benefits are claimed by practitioners and beauty influencers rather than measured in trials; the only physiological study cited here looked at skin and subcutis microcirculation in healthy subjects, not at facial shape. [1][2]

A 2007 pilot study in healthy subjects measured gua sha's effects on surface-tissue microcirculation, seeking to elucidate physiological mechanisms behind the effects observed clinically. [2] Wikipedia states that gua sha lacks high-quality evidence of clinical benefit and cites critics including Mark Crislip (2015), Edzard Ernst (2019) and William Mitchell (2026). [1] No published trial of facial gua sha for contour or appearance is cited in the Wikipedia article.

Nearly every treatment causes some skin trauma such as redness, bruising or dermatitis; burns and blood in the urine have been reported, and rare serious harms include brain bleeding and injuries requiring skin grafts. Infection is a concern with unsterilised tools or open wounds, though no bloodborne transmission has been directly linked to the practice. [1]

In the 1980s some Vietnamese immigrants in the United States distrusted Western providers partly from fear of being reported for child abuse after performing cạo gió on their children, and health providers in areas with large Southeast Asian populations, such as Orange County, California, often see sha marks that have been mistaken for abuse. [1] US physicians are required to report suspected abuse whatever the cultural context. [1] The 2001 Hong Kong film The Gua Sha Treatment centres on a welfare agency misreading such marks on a Chinese-American child. [1]
Some US states include gua sha in TCM licensing laws, which Bellamy (2018) criticised in Science-Based Medicine. [1]
